messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 21
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Public Defender
  trauma_type: Refugee
  pcl5: 62

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Thought Monitoring: constantly monitor own thoughts for signs of going crazy, Avoid Talking: Talking with others about the event or its aftermath, Avoid Reminders: Being reminded of the event by others
  Threat: Startle to Sounds: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people, Threat in Silence: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen, False Alarms: I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong
  Memory: Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images., Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred., Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
  Negative Appraisals: World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place, Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time, Constant Vigilance: I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Elias was nineteen when the shelling began in his hometown. He had been ushered into the stone-walled cellar beneath his family’s apartment, the heavy iron door sealing them into damp darkness. For hours, there was only the muffled thud of distant impacts, a silence so absolute it pressed against his eardrums. Then the ground shuddered, glass shattered upstairs, and boots pounded on the stairs. He folded himself onto the concrete floor, knees drawn to his chest, shoulders hunched against the cold stone, breathing in shallow, controlled pulls until the footsteps passed. He survived because he stayed quiet, stayed low, and stayed alert. What he knew then was that safety was an illusion and danger arrived without warning. After relocating to the United States as a refugee, he navigated resettlement services and eventually entered an accelerated legal training program, now working as a Public Defender in a state office. The cellar did not leave him. His mind never stopped scanning. He came to believe the world was a dangerous place, that he had to be on guard all the time, especially careful because you never knew what could happen next. In his daily work, every ring, echo, and sudden door slam demanded a response. An unusual silence in a room would tighten his chest immediately; he was certain something dangerous was about to happen. When a stapler clicked in his office or a car backfired on the street, his shoulders would jerk, his breath would catch, and his pulse would race as if the iron door were closing again. He would often find himself stepping back from a doorway, reacting as if he were in danger even when nothing was actually wrong. The past did not visit him as a narrative. It arrived as photographs: the grain of the cellar floor, the rusted hinge, the sliver of light that had cut through the crack beneath it. When those images surfaced, his body mirrored the old posture instantly, knees tight, spine curved, muscles locked in the same cramped alignment he had held for hours. Other times, the terror would wash over him without any clear picture, just the raw, unfiltered weight of the fear he had felt that night. Beside these reactions, Elias began watching his own mind with relentless precision. He monitored his thoughts constantly, searching for any sign that he was going crazy, counting his words, noting his breath, checking his focus like a man inspecting a structural beam for hairline fractures. He would not talk with others about the event or its aftermath, deflecting gentle questions about his past or changing the subject when colleagues mentioned the conflicts in his former country. Being reminded of the event by others was something he avoided carefully, steering conversations toward procedural deadlines or courtroom logistics instead. His work placed him inside the very environment where his sensitivities surfaced most sharply. During court recesses, Elias would sit in the unused overflow room; the absence of sound would tighten his chest, and he was certain something dangerous was about to happen. He mapped his caseload around predictable rhythms, turning down last-minute client meetings that required him to sit in closed offices where he could not monitor the entrance. His partner, Mara, had noticed how he pulled back. When she asked if he wanted to talk about what was weighing on him, he would shake his head and say he was just tired, then retreat to the other side of the living room to review case files. He had come to believe that staying close to the evidence was safer than leaning into uncertainty, but the distance between them grew with every avoided conversation. At twenty-one, Elias walked into a community mental health clinic because the volume of his own reactions had begun to interfere with his ability to function. He had missed two critical filing deadlines after becoming so fixated on a sudden noise outside his office window that he lost the thread of his afternoon. What frightened him most was not the memories themselves, but the way his body obeyed them before his mind could catch up, and the fear that he was fracturing under the weight of it all. He sat in the intake room with his hands folded tightly in his lap, hoping to find a way to lower the volume on the alarms he could not turn off, and wondering if anyone could help him stop waiting for the next blow.
